The authors suggest that no controlled study has reported a body temperature above 40 degrees possibly because volunteers had moderate single doses at rest, were well hydrated and were not in a hot or crowded environment, unlike some recreational settings. In their research setting a research assistant is always present, similar to a therapy session and unlike some other experimental settings; participants typically had no or very little earlier MDMA experience; the response may differ in people with psychiatric disorders compared with volunteers screened to be psychiatrically healthy; limits: only psychiatrically healthy and mostly young volunteers; hyponatraemia, neurocognitive function and long-term problems not assessed; 166 sessions of MDMA alone (278 counting those with a pretreatment drug) too few to exclude infrequent (0.1 to 1%) or rare (below 0.1%) events.

32 healthy volunteers (16 men, 16 women), mean age 25 (SD 3; range 20 to 31), from the University of Basel campus; excluded: a personal or first-degree-relative history of psychiatric disorder or chronic or acute physical illness, smoking, illicit drug use more than five times in a lifetime (past cannabis excepted) and any in the last 2 months (urine tests); 22 completely new to MDMA and 10 with fewer than five earlier uses; 19 had used cannabis more than five times and 15 other illicit drugs one to four times; women were tested in the follicular phase. Double-blind, placebo-controlled, random-order crossover; MDMA 125 mg (mean 1.89 mg/kg, SD 0.30) and identical placebo capsules, at least 10 days apart; registered (NCT01386177 and NCT01465685); paid. Visual analogue scales for 'happy', 'open' and 'close to others', and the 60-item Adjective Mood Rating Scale (AMRS); repeated measures were expressed as the peak change from baseline.

Empathy test: MDMA raised explicit and implicit emotional empathy ratings across all volunteers (F(1,31) = 6.05, P = 0.019; 4.29, P = 0.047), significantly for positive scenes (8.60, P = 0.006; 5.02, P = 0.032) and not for negative scenes; interaction with sex for implicit empathy (4.68, P = 0.039) and a trend for explicit (3.03, P = 0.092); post hoc, the rises were significant in men only (P = 0.025 explicit, 0.022 implicit); cognitive empathy unchanged. Money allocation (Social Value Orientation): the prosocial angle rose (F(1,31) = 4.42, P = 0.044) with a sex interaction (5.52, P = 0.026); post hoc significant in men (P = 0.008) and not in women; the inequality-aversion index tended to fall, analysed only in the subjects with a prosocial orientation (F(1,20) = 3.39, P = 0.079). Face recognition: accuracy fell overall (F(1,31) = 28.63, P < 0.001), for fearful (14.90), angry (18.60), disgusted (5.81, P = 0.022) and surprised (9.79, P = 0.004) faces but not happy faces (0.27, P = 0.607); the fall was significant in women and not in men.
